children.author: defrost
children.text:
I'm in a rural area (West Australian Wheat belt) and the local town has a "Sock Shop" that does a good trade with tourists on the weekends.

The local school routinely has classes working with the ladies of the sock shop working on aspects of making socks.

They make socks, without power, from sheep.

They cover everything from sheep and wool types, feed, making shears, shearing, carding, spinning, making wheels, things with treadles, dyes, knitting etc.

They also make socks with power, using Busi Sock Knitting machines from Italy.

We cover tech in farming in schools, from chain dragging and stump jumpers, to drones and Ag-Bots, and drag the kids out to the farming tech museums to walk them through the sheep shearing robots we built in the 1980s.

source.text:
"A man can work from sun to sun, but a woman's work is never done."

The spinning, particularly before spinning wheels became common (and affordable), could be done in parallel to a lot of other tasks - cooking (the waiting portions), walking to town or the fields, watching small children, and once you're used to it, can be done without light.

Making yarn from raw wool is my main hobby, and I've fallen into the annual rhythm of sourcing, sorting and scouring (cleaning to remove dirt and excess lanolin) wool in the summer when it's warm enough to suint (ferment the dirty wool in its own sweat, which works way better than it sounds) and then dry the wool outside, carding/combing and spinning in the fall and winter, and finally dyeing the finished yarn mostly in the spring, because I don't want to handle those chemicals indoors... and also so I have something nice to give the people I get the next set of fleeces from, beginning the cycle again.

I think we, as a society, have forgotten just how much time went into yarn/thread production before the Industrial Revolution because that was the first major automation target, and most women were happy not to have to do it any more. Plus, being mostly women's work, the details weren't important enough to the people who wrote "serious" books about the economy.
